I now have enough material to compile the verse-by-verse notes. Let me organize what the various sources say.

---

## Acts 27:1-22 — Verse-by-Verse Commentary Notes

### v. 1 — *“When it was decided that we would sail for Italy, Paul and some other prisoners were handed over to a centurion named Julius, who belonged to the Imperial Regiment.”*

- **“We” marks the final and longest “we-section”** in Acts (27:1–28:16), indicating Luke was an eyewitness on this voyage. Luke likely remained with Paul throughout his two-year Caesarean detention. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/acts-27.html
- **The decision to sail was made by Festus** pursuant to Paul’s appeal to Caesar, yet behind it stood the will of God, who had already promised Paul he would testify in Rome (Acts 23:11). — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/acts/27.htm
- **Julius was a centurion of the “Augustan Cohort” (or “Imperial Regiment”).** The exact identity of this cohort is debated. It may have been a cohort of the Syrian legions bearing the honorary title “Augustan,” or one responsible for communications between the emperor and provincial armies. The title was given to multiple cohorts. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/acts-27.html
- **“Some other prisoners”** were likely condemned criminals being sent to Rome to die in the arena, unlike Paul who was an uncondemned citizen awaiting trial. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-27/
- **The Greek verb *paradidomi* (“handed over”) conveys giving someone into the power of another.** Paul was delivered into Roman custody, yet under God’s sovereign hand. — https://www.preceptaustin.org/acts-27-commentary

**Tradition note — Reformed/Evangelical:** Kent (quoted in Constable) stresses divine sovereignty: “The means were not what Paul could have foreseen nor what he might have chosen, but God was in control and the apostle was fully willing to leave the details in His hands.” — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/acts-27.html

---

### v. 2 — *“We boarded an Adramyttian ship about to sail for ports along the coast of Asia, and we put out to sea. Aristarchus, a Macedonian from Thessalonica, was with us.”*

- **The ship was a coastal vessel from Adramyttium**, a seaport of Mysia opposite Lesbos (about 110 miles north of Ephesus). It would stop at ports along the northeastern Mediterranean coast. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/acts-27.html
- **Gill notes** two possible locations for Adramyttium: one in Mysia (Asia Minor) and another in Africa (Hadrumetum). He leans toward the Mysian port since the ship stopped at Myra in Lycia. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/acts/27.htm
- **Aristarchus** had been with Paul since at least the Ephesian riot (Acts 19:29). He, along with Luke, stayed with Paul during his Caesarean imprisonment and would travel with him all the way to Rome (Colossians 4:10; Philemon 24). Their presence probably contributed to the respect shown Paul. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/acts-27.html
- **The favor Paul enjoyed from Julius** (v. 3) meant he was allowed to take these companions. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-27/

---

### v. 3 — *“The next day we landed at Sidon, and Julius treated Paul with consideration, allowing him to visit his friends and receive their care.”*

- **Sidon** lay about 70 miles north of Caesarea on the Phoenician coast. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/acts-27.html
- **“Friends”** were likely members of a church there (cf. Acts 11:19, where those scattered after Stephen’s martyrdom went as far as Phoenicia). — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/acts-27.html
- **Julius treated Paul with *philanthrōpōs* (kindly/humanely).** Ellicott comments that this centurion, like others in Acts (Cornelius, the centurion in Acts 22:26, the one in 24:23), displays Roman military decency. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/acts/27.htm
- **Gill** notes that Julius allowed Paul “to go to his friends and receive care” — probably refreshment and provisions for the voyage from the Christians at Sidon. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/acts/27.htm
- **Enduring Word** notes that Paul’s godly character and Christian love earned him genuine respect from a Roman soldier, and Paul was different from the other prisoners — not yet condemned, but awaiting trial. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-27/

---

### v. 4 — *“After putting out from there, we sailed to the lee of Cyprus because the winds were against us.”*

- **Prevailing winds** in the Mediterranean during this season (autumn) typically blow from west to east or from the northwest. This forced the ship to sail on the **eastern (lee) side of Cyprus** for shelter, rather than the direct open-sea route south of Cyprus. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/acts-27.html
- **This is the opposite route** Paul had taken earlier (Acts 21:1–3), when sailing from Patara to Tyre he passed south of Cyprus. Now the contrary winds dictated a different course. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-27/
- **Traditional reading:** The winds were “contrary” — a picture of how God’s providence often leads through difficulty. The journey toward God’s promised destination (Rome) was not smooth. — https://www.preceptaustin.org/acts-27-commentary

---

### v. 5 — *“And when we had sailed across the open sea off the coast of Cilicia and Pamphylia, we came to Myra in Lycia.”*

- **The ship sailed northward** along the eastern side of Cyprus, then across the open water past Cilicia and Pamphylia to **Myra**, a port city in Lycia (southern Asia Minor, modern Turkey). — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/acts-27.html
- **This leg was about 500 miles** and took approximately 14 days. — https://www.preceptaustin.org/acts-27-commentary
- **Myra** was an important trans-shipment port where larger vessels bound for Italy could be found. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/acts/27.htm

---

### v. 6 — *“There the centurion found an Alexandrian ship sailing for Italy and put us on board.”*

- **This was a grain freighter** from Alexandria, Egypt — part of the fleet that supplied Rome with Egyptian grain. According to contemporary descriptions, these ships could be 180 feet long, 50 feet wide, and 44 feet deep from deck to hold. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/acts-27.html
- **Hughes (quoted in Enduring Word)** says a typical grain freighter was 140 feet long, 36 feet wide, had one mast with a large square sail, and steered with two paddle-like rudders at the stern. Because of its design, it could not sail into the wind. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-27/
- **Julius transferred his prisoners** to this ship because it was going directly to Italy — a providential connection. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/acts/27.htm

---

### v. 7 — *“After sailing slowly for many days, we arrived off Cnidus. When the wind impeded us, we sailed to the lee of Crete, opposite Salmone.”*

- **Cnidus** stood at the southwestern tip of Asia Minor, where the Aegean meets the Mediterranean, about 108 miles south of Ephesus. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/acts-27.html
- **The northwesterly wind** prevented them from continuing westward, forcing them to turn south under the shelter of Crete, rounding **Cape Salmone** (the island’s easternmost point). — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/acts-27.html
- The phrase **“sailing slowly”** and **“with difficulty”** (v. 8) sets the tone: their progress is increasingly laborious as winter approaches. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-27/

**Tradition note — Reformed/Piper (Desiring God):** John Piper notes the repeated language of difficulty and opposition in vv. 4, 7–9 as a picture of the believer’s life: “the winds were against us… we sailed slowly… arrived with difficulty… the voyage was now dangerous.” God’s promises do not guarantee smooth sailing. — https://www.desiringgod.org/articles/god-will-bring-you-through

---

### v. 8 — *“After we had moved along the coast with difficulty, we came to a place called Fair Havens, near the town of Lasea.”*

- **Fair Havens** (probably modern Limeonas Kalous) was a small bay on the southern coast of Crete near the town of **Lasea**. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/acts-27.html
- **The name “Fair Havens” was somewhat ironic**, because while it offered a safe anchorage in fair weather, its position left it exposed to winter winds. Enduring Word notes that one commentator suggests “the local Chamber of Commerce named the place.” — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-27/
- **Gill** notes that Fair Havens is mentioned by other ancient geographers and was known as a harbor on Crete’s southern coast. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/acts/27.htm

---

### v. 9 — *“By now much time had passed, and the voyage had already become dangerous because it was after the Fast. So Paul advised them…”*

- **“The Fast”** is unanimously identified by commentators as the **Day of Atonement (Yom Kippur)**, which falls in late September or early October. In AD 59, the likely year of this voyage, it fell around October 5. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-27/
- **Bruce (quoted in Enduring Word):** “The dangerous season for sailing began about September 14 and lasted until November 11; after the latter date all navigation on the open sea came to an end until winter was over.” — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-27/
- **Constable:** People considered it dangerous to travel by sea between mid-September and mid-November, and harbors closed for winter from mid-November to mid-February. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/acts-27.html
- **Luke’s reference to the Fast** suggests he was writing partly for a Jewish or God-fearing audience who would recognize the Jewish calendar reference. It also anchors the narrative historically. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/acts/27.htm

**Denominational note — Pentecostal/Charismatic (Enduring Word / David Guzik):** Paul’s advice in v. 10 was “grounded in his extensive Mediterranean travel experience and three previous shipwrecks, not necessarily a prophetic word.” — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-27/

**Contrasting view — older commentators (Benson, Ellicott):** Some older commentators see Paul’s perception as more than mere experience. Benson says Paul “foresaw and foretold” the disaster, and the hearers “ought to have believed his prediction… especially as Luke and Aristarchus… could have borne witness to the spirit of prophecy… with which he was endowed.” — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/rbc/acts-27.html (archived previously)

---

### v. 10 — *“Men, I can see that our voyage will be filled with disaster and great loss, not only to ship and cargo, but to our own lives as well.”*

- **“I perceive” (theōreō):** Paul used a verb meaning “I see/observe.” The question is whether this was natural observation or spiritual insight. The Preacher’s Homiletical Commentary notes: “The apostle apprehended, not from supernatural guidance, but from the exercise of his own judgment, looking to the lateness of the season… that to proceed further would only result in disaster.” — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/phc/acts-27.html
- **Paul had extensive sea experience:** 2 Corinthians 11:25 records three previous shipwrecks and a night and a day adrift at sea before this voyage. Haenchen calculated Paul traveled at least 3,000 miles by sea in Acts alone. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/acts-27.html
- **“Not only… ship and cargo, but… our own lives”:** Paul predicted loss of life, which is noteworthy — at this point he had no angelic assurance of anyone’s safety (contrast v. 23–24). His warning about loss of life did not ultimately come true because of God’s merciful intervention, not because Paul was a false prophet. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-27/

---

### v. 11 — *“But contrary to Paul’s advice, the centurion was persuaded by the pilot and by the owner of the ship.”*

- **The centurion had the final say** as the senior Roman officer responsible for the prisoners and the transport. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/acts-27.html
- **The “pilot” (kybernētēs) was the ship’s master/helmsman** and the **owner (nauklēros)** was likely the ship’s owner or the agent representing the grain fleet. Both had strong financial motives to reach Rome before winter closure. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/acts/27.htm
- **Ellicott:** “The centurion believed the master and the owner of the ship, more than those things which were spoken by Paul.” — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/acts/27.htm

**Application note — Preacher’s Homiletical Commentary:** “The mistake committed by the centurion.—He gave more heed to the master and the owner of the ship than to those things which were spoken by Paul.” This is a picture of how worldly expertise often drowns out godly counsel. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/phc/acts-27.html

---

### v. 12 — *“Since the harbor was unsuitable to winter in, the majority decided to sail on, if somehow they could reach Phoenix to winter there. Phoenix was a harbor in Crete facing both southwest and northwest.”*

- **Fair Havens was “unsuitable”** because the bay was exposed to winter winds and storms. It was also a small, dull town — not a place 276 people wanted to spend months. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-27/
- **Phoenix** (modern Phineka, or possibly Lutro) was only about 40–45 miles farther west along the Cretan coast. It offered a better-protected harbor that faced southwest and northwest. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/acts-27.html
- **“The majority decided”:** The decision was made by vote, likely of the crew and officers, but the centurion ratified it. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-27/
- **The Greek phrase** describing Phoenix’s harbor orientation has been debated — some manuscripts differ. The harbor likely opened toward the southwest and northwest, offering protection from winter storms. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/acts/27.htm

---

### v. 13 — *“When a gentle south wind began to blow, they thought they had their opportunity. So they weighed anchor and sailed along, hugging the coast of Crete.”*

- **The gentle south wind** seemed to confirm their decision. It appeared providential — favorable weather for the short 40-mile trip to Phoenix. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-27/
- **“They thought they had their opportunity”:** This phrase captures the deceptive nature of circumstances. What looked like answered desire was actually the setup for disaster. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/acts-27.html
- **“Hugging the coast”** — they stayed close to Crete’s shoreline, a prudent measure for coastal sailing. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-27/

**Tradition note — Reformed (Piper/Desiring God):** This moment of apparent calm is a picture of how we can mistake favorable circumstances for God’s green light, when God had already given clear warning through Paul to stay put. — https://www.desiringgod.org/articles/god-will-bring-you-through

---

### v. 14 — *“But it was not long before a cyclone called the Northeaster swept down across the island.”*

- **The Greek name for this wind** varies in manuscripts. The traditional reading is **“Euroclydon”** (KJV), meaning a tempestuous northeastern wind. Some manuscripts read **“Euraquilo”** (a hybrid Latin-Greek term for “northeaster”). Modern versions tend toward “Northeaster.” — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-27/
- **This wind was notorious** among ancient Mediterranean sailors for its sudden, violent, destructive power. It “swept down” (literally “rushed down”) from the Cretan mountains. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/acts-27.html
- **The sudden shift** from gentle south wind to violent northeaster is typical of the Mediterranean autumn. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/acts/27.htm

---

### v. 15 — *“Unable to head into the wind, the ship was caught up. So we gave way and let ourselves be driven along.”*

- **Ancient ships could not tack** (sail into the wind) effectively, especially not a large grain freighter with a single square sail. Once caught, the only option was to surrender to the wind. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/acts-27.html
- **“Gave way”** — the Greek implies they yielded all control. They were entirely at the mercy of the storm. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-27/

---

### v. 16 — *“Passing to the lee of a small island called Cauda, we barely managed to secure the lifeboat.”*

- **Cauda (or Clauda)** is modern Gavdos (or Gozzo), about 23 miles south of Crete. It provided brief shelter in its lee. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/acts-27.html
- **The “lifeboat” (skiff/dinghy)** was normally towed behind the ship. In storm conditions, it needed to be hauled aboard to prevent it from being lost or smashed. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-27/
- **“Barely managed”:** Luke’s description is vivid and personal. Enduring Word suggests “the doctor was probably pressed into service pulling ropes.” — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-27/

---

### v. 17 — *“After hoisting it up, the crew used ropes to undergird the ship. And fearing that they would run aground on the sandbars of Syrtis, they lowered the sea anchor and were driven along.”*

- **“Undergird the ship” (hypozōnnymi):** Cables or ropes were passed under the hull and tightened to reinforce the ship’s timbers against the pounding waves — a standard ancient emergency measure known as “frapping.” — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-27/
- **The Syrtis** (modern Gulf of Sidra off Libya) was a dreaded region of quicksands and shoals. The northeaster was driving them directly toward it. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/acts-27.html
- **“Lowered the sea anchor”** — there is some debate about what exactly was lowered. The Greek term (*skeuos*) simply means “gear/equipment.” Constable suggests it may refer to sails, rigging, or a sea anchor (drogue) deployed to slow the ship. The BSB renders it “sea anchor.” — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/acts-27.html

**Denominational/scholarly note — NET Bible (modern scholarship):** Some scholars argue the term refers to letting down the mainsail or reducing sail, not a sea anchor, since ancient ships did not typically carry drogues. The sense is that they reduced sail to let the ship be driven by the wind while keeping some control. — (This is a well-known scholarly discussion, though the NET page was not directly fetched.)

---

### v. 18 — *“We were tossed so violently that the next day the men began to jettison the cargo.”*

- **The violence of the storm** forced the crew to throw cargo overboard to lighten the ship — likely the grain that was the ship’s commercial freight. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-27/
- **Constable:** “Evidently the ship was taking on so much water that the captain decided to jettison the wheat on board as well as other cargo.” — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/acts-27.html
- **This parallels Jonah 1:5**, where the sailors threw cargo overboard to save their ship — a deliberate literary parallel Luke may be drawing. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/acts-27.html

---

### v. 19 — *“On the third day, they threw the ship’s tackle overboard with their own hands.”*

- **“With their own hands”:** The phrase emphasizes that passengers and crew alike participated — not just the sailors. The situation was so desperate that everyone helped strip the ship. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-27/
- **“Ship’s tackle”** refers to the spare gear, rigging, and equipment necessary for sailing — throwing it overboard meant abandoning any pretense of navigating the ship. They were now purely drifting. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/acts/27.htm

---

### v. 20 — *“When neither sun nor stars appeared for many days and the great storm continued to batter us, we abandoned all hope of being saved.”*

- **Before the compass**, the sun by day and stars by night were the only navigational guides. Without them for “many days,” the sailors had no idea where they were. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/acts/27.htm
- **Ellicott adds:** The total despair “implies some other cause of fear in addition to the mere violence of the gale, and the successive attempts to lighten the ship make it all but certain that she had sprung a leak, which their efforts were powerless to stop.” — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/acts/27.htm
- **“All hope… was abandoned”:** This is total, final despair — 276 people, including Paul, Luke, and Aristarchus, had given up. Constable notes this sets the stage for God’s intervention at the lowest human point. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/acts-27.html
- **Benson** says: “The whole ship’s company expected nothing but that the ship would certainly be lost, and we should all perish with it.” — (Benson’s Commentary, previously accessed)

**Tradition note — Spurgeon (Baptist):** In his sermon on this passage, Spurgeon observes that this was the moment the believer comes to the front: “Paul is nothing but a prisoner all the time the ship sails safely… but the storm comes on… and he who was only a prisoner becomes practically the chief man in the ship.” — https://www.spurgeon.org/sermons/paul-in-the-tempest

---

### v. 21 — *“After the men had gone a long time without food, Paul stood up among them and said, ‘Men, you should have followed my advice not to sail from Crete. Then you would have averted this disaster and loss.’”*

- **“Long time without food” (long abstinence):** This was not a spiritual fast but likely due to seasickness, the impossibility of cooking in the storm, and perhaps rationing because they did not know how long supplies would last. Ellicott says they were “put on reduced rations” and “cooking was all but impossible.” — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/acts/27.htm
- **Paul’s “I told you so”** is interpreted by Constable not as gloating, but as establishing credibility: “What he had predicted had taken place, and what he was about to predict would also.” — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/acts-27.html
- **Bible.org (Bob Utley):** “This is Paul’s ‘I told you so!’ It provided Paul the opportunity to act as the Spirit’s spokesman.” — (from earlier search excerpt of bible.org)
- **Ellicott:** “With the feeling natural to one whose counsel had been slighted, he reminds them that if they had followed it they would have been spared the harm and loss.” — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/acts/27.htm
- **Enduring Word:** “Paul could not resist (rightly so) an ‘I told you so’ moment.” — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-27/

**Denominational note — Pentecostal/Charismatic:** Enduring Word emphasizes this was not Paul being petty; his point “wasn’t simply to tell them he was right, but to bring them good news.” — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-27/

---

### v. 22 — *“But now I urge you to keep up your courage, because you will not experience any loss of life, but only of the ship.”*

- **“Keep up your courage” (euthymeō):** The same verb form used in Acts 23:11 when Jesus told Paul to “take courage.” Paul now passes that divine encouragement on to others. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/acts-27.html
- **Ellicott:** “Look and tone, we may well believe, helped the words. It was something in that scene of misery and dejection to see one man stand forward with a brave, calm confidence.” — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/acts/27.htm
- **“No loss of life… but only of the ship”:** This was “a mixed message.” The promise that no life would be lost was hard to believe if the ship was to be destroyed. It was also bad news commercially — the cargo was already gone (v. 18) and now the ship itself would be lost. But humanly speaking, what mattered was survival. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-27/
- **Benson** adds a conditional note: “provided they would do as he directed them, see Acts 27:31. In God’s promises there is generally implied a tacit condition.” — (Benson, previously accessed)
- **The Church Pulpit Commentary** notes this as “Good Cheer in the Storm” and identifies Paul’s situation as: (a) well-nigh hopeless, (b) brought about by no fault of his — Paul was in the right path, “greatest trials often when we are in path of duty,” (c) seeming to contradict God’s revealed purpose (Acts 23:11). — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cpc/acts-27.html

**Tradition note — Reformed/Baptist (Piper, Desiring God):** Piper emphasizes that Paul’s confidence in vv. 21–22 flowed from the *old promise*, not a new one: “In the midst of Paul’s terrifying storm, he didn’t need a new promise or a new revelation — he needed to remember the promise God had already given.” God had already told Paul he would testify in Rome (Acts 23:11); therefore, he could not die at sea. — https://www.desiringgod.org/articles/god-will-bring-you-through

**Tradition note — Lutheran (LCMS):** While no directly fetched LCMS page is available, Lutheran commentators typically emphasize that this passage illustrates God’s means of grace operating through a called servant. Paul functions as a “pastor” to the ship’s company — preaching repentance (v. 21) and then gospel consolation (v. 22). The pattern is law (you should have listened) followed by gospel (take heart, you will be saved).

---

### Summary of Key Theological/Didactic Points Across Traditions

| Theme | Common Reading | Distinctive Variations |
|---|---|---|
| **Paul’s counsel (vv. 9–10)** | Based on experience and wisdom; possibly also prophetic | Pentecostal (Enduring Word): “not necessarily a prophetic word” / Older commentators (Benson): likely prophetic insight |
| **Sovereignty and human means** | God’s promise (v. 22–24) operated through ordinary means (sailors staying aboard, eating food) | Reformed (Constable/Kent): stresses “divine sovereignty and human responsibility” as complementary / Baptist (Spurgeon): the believer rises to leadership in crisis |
| **The “I told you so” (v. 21)** | Legitimate credibility-establishment, not gloating | Evangelical consensus: Paul spoke to gain a hearing for the good news to follow |
| **“No loss of life” (v. 22)** | A divine promise revealed through an angel (vv. 23–24) | Benson: implies a tacit condition (obedience to Paul’s later directions) / Piper: rooted in the older promise of Acts 23:11 |
| **The storm as spiritual metaphor** | The Christian life includes storms; faith shines brightest in darkness | Piper: storms strip away false hopes so only God’s word remains / Spurgeon: the believer becomes “the center of the whole company” when all human hope fails |
